description.en: Pythonic error handling flips the script: don't check first — try, and handle the failure. Learn EAFP and write cleaner, faster code that reads like intent.

story_variants.en:
## The Pythonic Way to Fail

"Many languages say *Look Before You Leap* (LBYL) — check every condition before acting," Vaathiyaar says. "Python prefers **EAFP: Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission**. Just *try* the operation, and catch the exception if it fails. It's cleaner, and it avoids a subtle bug: between your check and your action, the world can change."

### LBYL vs EAFP

```
# LBYL — brittle, races
if key in d and isinstance(d[key], dict) and inner in d[key]:
    value = d[key][inner]

# EAFP — clean intent
try:
    value = d[key][inner]
except (KeyError, TypeError):
    value = None
```

EAFP states the happy path plainly, then handles what can go wrong. It's especially natural for nested lookups, file access, and type coercion — anywhere a pre-check would be long, repetitive, or racy.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** reach for `try/except` before a wall of `if` guards. Let the exception tell you what went wrong, and handle exactly that.

Today you implement `get_nested(d, path)` the EAFP way — walk a list of keys and return `None` the moment any step fails.

explanation.en: Start at the top of the structure
Just index — don't pre-check it exists
Any missing key or wrong type -> gracefully return None

instruction.en: Implement `get_nested(d, path)` using EAFP: walk the list of keys in `path` into the nested dict `d`, returning the value if it exists, or `None` if any key is missing or a step isn't indexable (catch `KeyError`/`TypeError`). Then print `get_nested({'a': {'b': 42}}, ['a', 'b'])` (expected: `42`).

practice_challenges.starter_code:
def get_nested(d: dict, path: list):
    """Walk `path` into `d` the EAFP way; return None on any failure."""
    # try: walk each key; except (KeyError, TypeError): return None
    pass

print(get_nested({'a': {'b': 42}}, ['a', 'b']))

en: Wrap the whole walk in try/except
Loop: cur = cur[key] for each key in path

q.en: What does the EAFP style of error handling mean in Python?
q.ta: Python-இல் EAFP பாணி பிழை கையாளுதல் என்றால் என்ன?

en: Validate all input first so no exception is ever raised
Check every condition with if before acting
Try the operation and catch the exception if it fails
Let every exception crash the program so you see it
ta: எந்த விதிவிலக்கும் வராதபடி முதலில் எல்லா உள்ளீட்டையும் சரிபார்ப்பது
செயல்படும் முன் ஒவ்வொரு நிபந்தனையையும் if மூலம் சரிபார்ப்பது
செயலை முயற்சி செய்து, தோல்வியடைந்தால் விதிவிலக்கைப் பிடிப்பது
பிழை தெரிய, ஒவ்வொரு விதிவிலக்கும் நிரலை நிறுத்த விடுவது

q.en: Which subtle bug can an LBYL check-then-act approach have that EAFP avoids?
q.ta: EAFP தவிர்க்கும், ஆனால் LBYL 'முதலில் சரிபார், பின் செயல்படு' முறையில் வரக்கூடிய நுட்பமான பிழை எது?

en: LBYL code always runs the action twice
if statements cannot test whether a key is in a dict
Things can change between the check and the action
Checks silently convert values to the wrong type
ta: LBYL குறியீடு எப்போதும் செயலை இரண்டு முறை இயக்கும்
ஒரு key dict-இல் உள்ளதா என்று if ஆல் சோதிக்க முடியாது
சரிபார்ப்புகள் மதிப்புகளைத் தவறான வகைக்கு மறைமுகமாக மாற்றும்

q.en: Using the lesson's get_nested (catching KeyError and TypeError), what does get_nested({'a': 5}, ['a', 'b']) return?
q.ta: பாடத்தின் get_nested (KeyError, TypeError பிடிக்கும்) பயன்படுத்தினால், get_nested({'a': 5}, ['a', 'b']) என்ன திருப்பும்?

under_the_hood.summary: Since CPython 3.11 a try block costs almost nothing when no exception occurs, so EAFP pays only when a lookup fails, while LBYL repeats every lookup and can race with changes between the check and the use.

steps.title: LBYL does the work twice
steps.body: `if key in d and isinstance(d[key], dict) and inner in d[key]: value = d[key][inner]` hashes `key` and probes the dict three times, then once more for the real access. Each check is a separate operation, and the code grows with every level of nesting.

left.label: LBYL (check first)
left.code:
if key in d and \
   isinstance(d[key], dict) and \
   inner in d[key]:
    value = d[key][inner]
else:
    value = None

right.label: EAFP (just try)

steps.title: EAFP does each lookup once
steps.body: `d[key][inner]` performs exactly the two lookups it needs. If both succeed, the result is used directly. In CPython 3.11, entering the try costs no extra instructions; the compiler records the protected range in an exception table instead.

stepDescriptions.description: Happy path: two subscript operations, nothing else.
On failure, the exception table sends control here; the tuple is checked with isinstance.
Fallback value for a missing or non-dict level.

steps.title: The failure path is the expensive one
steps.body: When a key is missing, Python creates a KeyError object, records a traceback entry and searches the exception table. That is more costly than a failed `in` check. So EAFP is the better deal when failures are uncommon; if most lookups fail, `.get()` or a check can be faster.

values: miss: lookup + exception object + handler search

steps.title: No gap for the world to change
steps.body: With LBYL there is a moment between `os.path.exists(p)` and `open(p)` when another process can delete the file (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). `try: open(p) except FileNotFoundError:` asks the OS once, so the answer cannot go stale.

steps.title: Keep the try narrow
steps.body: Put only the risky operation inside the try and catch only the exceptions you expect. A broad try around many lines could catch a KeyError from an unrelated bug and hide it behind your fallback value.

under_the_hood.takeaway: EAFP is cheap when things usually work and avoids check-then-use races. Wrap the one operation that can fail, name the exceptions you expect, and let everything else surface.
